1. Core Clinical Tension: A 29-year-old woman presented with persistent pelvic discomfort, abdominal distension, dysuria, and cachexia (BMI 16 kg/m2) over 8 months, refractory to multiple courses of empiric antibiotics. Imaging showed bilateral complex cystic adnexal masses, ascites, and peritoneal thickening, mimicking advanced ovarian carcinoma or chronic pelvic inflammatory disease, but representing isolated peritoneal tuberculosis.
2. Admission Breakpoint: The admission breakpoint occurs upon admission to gynecology following initial transvaginal ultrasound, pelvic CT, and baseline laboratory evaluation (showing mild CRP elevation, normal leukocytes, negative beta-hCG, and elevated CA125), prior to diagnostic laparoscopy and peritoneal biopsy/mycobacterial culture.
3. Differential Distinctions: Pelvic inflammatory disease / tubo-ovarian abscess was considered due to adnexal masses, pelvic pain, and cervical motion tenderness, but ruled out by repeated failure of empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics and negative STD screening; advanced ovarian carcinoma / peritoneal carcinomatosis was strongly suspected due to ascites, peritoneal nodules, and elevated CA125/CA15-3, but excluded by negative peritoneal cytology and absence of malignant histopathology; peritoneal tuberculosis was confirmed by laparoscopic findings of granulomatous peritonitis, elevated ascitic ADA (45.5 U/L), and positive culture for MTBC.
case_prompt:
A 29-year-old nulliparous Black woman presented to the emergency department complaining of persistent pelvic pain, abdominal distension, dysuria, and an unintentional 4-kg weight loss over the preceding eight months. She denied fever, dysmenorrhea, or abnormal vaginal discharge, but reported sporadic dyspareunia. Over the prior months, she had been treated empirically on multiple occasions for presumptive pelvic inflammatory disease and urinary tract infection with regimens including ceftriaxone, doxycycline, metronidazole, and cefuroxime, without clinical improvement. She had regular menstrual cycles and a normal cervical cancer screening from two years prior.

On physical examination, she was apyretic and normotensive, with a low body mass index of 16 kg/m2 and a chronically ill appearance. The abdomen was diffusely distended, slightly tender to palpation, and without palpable organomegaly. Speculum examination revealed non-specific vaginal discharge without cervical lesions. Bimanual pelvic examination elicited cervical and adnexal motion tenderness without palpable discrete pelvic masses.

Transvaginal ultrasound demonstrated a normal-sized uterus with bilateral anechoic, multiloculated cystic adnexal lesions measuring 81 x 73 mm on the left and 49 x 20 mm on the right, accompanied by ascites and peritoneal thickening. Baseline laboratory testing revealed a leukocyte count of 5,100/uL (57.2% neutrophils), a C-reactive protein level of 2.23 mg/L, and normal liver transaminases, urea, creatinine, and lactate dehydrogenase. Human chorionic gonadotropin was negative. Pelvic computed tomography confirmed bilateral adnexal cystic lesions, ascites, and peritoneal thickening, raising concerns for complicated pelvic inflammatory disease versus peritoneal carcinomatosis. Serum tumor markers showed CA125 elevated at 42.7 U/mL and CA15-3 at 60.4 U/mL, with normal CEA and CA19-9.
